hook.text: In 79 CE, Vesuvius buried Pompeii in ash. Bread stayed in ovens. Dogs stayed on chains. Time stopped instantly.

buildup.text: Pompeii was a Roman city preserved under volcanic ash, offering a snapshot of daily life frozen in a single moment.

discovery.text: Excavations revealed homes, shops, graffiti, food, and even body casts of people caught in the eruption.

twist.text: Pompeii isn't just tragedy tourism. It's the most complete picture of ordinary Roman life ever found.

climax.text: Pompeii reminds us that archaeology is at its best when it captures the everyday, not just the monumental.

punchline.text: Disaster preserved what time would have erased.

quiz.question: Why is Pompeii archaeologically important?
options: It had the largest Roman temple
Volcanic ash preserved a complete snapshot of daily life
It was the capital of the Roman Empire

details.summary: Pompeii was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE, preserving an entire Roman city in volcanic ash. The site provides an extraordinarily detailed snapshot of daily Roman life — from bakeries and brothels to graffiti and garden plans — frozen in a single moment.
details.whyItMatters: Pompeii offers an unparalleled archaeological window into ordinary ancient life. While most archaeology reconstructs patterns from fragments, Pompeii preserves complete buildings, meals in progress, and people in their final moments.
takeaways: Pompeii was preserved by Vesuvius eruption in 79 CE
It provides extraordinarily detailed evidence of daily Roman life
The site captures a complete city frozen in a single moment

faq.question: What makes Pompeii so valuable to archaeologists?
faq.answer: Normal archaeological sites are gradually abandoned, with valuables removed and structures repurposed. Pompeii was sealed instantly, preserving food on tables, paint on walls, organic materials that normally decay, and even the shapes of victims in their death poses.

faq.question: How much of Pompeii remains unexcavated?
faq.answer: Roughly one-third of Pompeii has never been excavated. Archaeologists are deliberately preserving these areas for future researchers with better techniques. Ongoing excavations continue to produce remarkable discoveries from the unexcavated portions.
